title: Money that never reaches a vote
question: How much of what the City contracts for sits below the line at which the Board of Supervisors must vote, and how has that share moved?
finding: Of 26,508 contracts on the City’s books that began in 2018 to 2026, worth $71.77 billion as agreed, 925 (3.5%) are large or long enough for the Board’s line to reach them; they hold $39.64 billion. The other 25,583 hold $32.13 billion, 45% of the dollars: $21.29 billion in 24,261 contracts under $10 million, and $10.84 billion in 1,322 construction contracts, which follow their own rules whatever their size. The share of dollars outside the line was 32% for contracts that began in 2019 and 51% for those that began in 2025. A separate screen counts 364 contracts sized between $9.5 million and $10 million against 39 just above (the “contract thresholds” results).
how: Every contract in the Controller’s Supplier Contracts table with an agreed amount, one record per contract number, grouped by the calendar year its term began. “Reached by the line” means an agreed amount of $10 million or more, or a term longer than ten years, which is how the ballot summary in the case file states the rule as it stood before the November 2026 measure. Contracts typed as construction are shown apart: the Budget and Legislative Analyst leaves them out of its own count and reports that they do not need Board approval except in special cases. Shares are of agreed dollars for contracts beginning that year.
limits: Delegation below a line is the design, not a loophole: the line was set by voters in 1988. A contract under it may still be approved by the department’s own commission, and the Controller’s 2020 review of contracting records that purchasing of goods and services is delegated to the City’s purchaser. The table shows today’s amounts, so an older contract has had more years to be amended past $10 million; part of any rise in the recent share is that recent contracts have not yet grown. A contract reached by the line is not proof that a vote was held, and one below it may have gone to the Board for another reason (a lease, a waiver, an approval after the fact). 2026 is a part year. What would settle the trend: the amount of each contract at award, which the table does not keep.
